sections.markdown:
## C2 — Confusable pairs and knowledge-graph hints: the two school bus speed rules, red versus blue lights, high versus low beams, look-alike parking distances and phone exceptions
Confusable pairs among stopping, emergency-vehicle, lighting and parking rules, followed by continuation facts the C block left out for size; each block ties to one handbook page, and hint metadata sits only in the trailing line of a block.

FACT_ID: sec07-R01 | anchor: A04
Two separate 10 mph rules apply to school buses: slow to 10 mph when you are across a safety island or raised median on a dual-lane highway, and pass at no more than 10 mph when the bus is stopped directly in front of a school. [A04]
Why it matters: group school buses; confusable median rule versus school-front rule.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0079]

FACT_ID: sec07-R02 | anchor: A05
A driver on the far side of a safety island or raised median on a dual highway does not have to stop for a frozen dessert truck. [A05]
Why it matters: group special vehicles; confusable dessert truck versus school bus beyond a median.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0080]

FACT_ID: sec07-R03 | anchor: A05
Police cars, fire trucks, ambulances and other emergency vehicles use sirens and red lights, while private vehicles of volunteer fire and rescue squad members answering a call, with emergency vehicle identification, use blue lights. [A05]
Why it matters: group emergency vehicles; confusable red versus blue lights.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0080]

FACT_ID: sec07-R04 | anchor: A05
Two emergency-vehicle distances are easy to swap: stay at least 300 feet behind a signaling emergency vehicle, and never park within 200 feet of a fire department vehicle in service. [A05]
Why it matters: group emergency vehicles; confusable three hundred versus two hundred feet.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0080]

FACT_ID: sec07-R05 | anchor: A08
High beams are for open country with no traffic in sight, while low beams are for city driving, heavier traffic, following another vehicle and meeting oncoming vehicles. [A08]
Why it matters: group headlights; confusable high versus low beam.
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0085]

FACT_ID: sec07-R06 | anchor: A10
Two different 20-foot no-parking rules exist: within 20 feet of the end of a pedestrian safety zone, and within 20 feet of a fire station driveway entrance. [A10]
Why it matters: group parking; confusable safety zone versus fire station.
Source: [A10 -> pdf-0087]

FACT_ID: sec07-R07 | anchor: A02
A driver must also stop when a traffic officer orders it, and at a yield sign when traffic does not allow a safe merge. [A02]
Why it matters: group stopping; difficulty low.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0077]

FACT_ID: sec07-R08 | anchor: A02
A driver must also stop when coming out of an alley, private driveway or building, and at a bridge span that is about to open for boats. [A02]
Why it matters: group stopping; difficulty medium.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0077]

FACT_ID: sec07-R09 | anchor: A03
A driver must stop for a pedestrian in a crosswalk or at an intersection, and for a motorized wheelchair or mobility-assistance device there. [A03]
Why it matters: group stopping; difficulty low.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0078]

FACT_ID: sec07-R10 | anchor: A03
Railroad crossing warnings can include advance-warning signs, pavement markings, flashing red lights, gates with or without flashing lights, ringing bells and flag signals. [A03]
Why it matters: group railroad crossings; difficulty low.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0078]

FACT_ID: sec07-R11 | anchor: A04
School buses turn on yellow or amber lights before stopping and red lights once stopped, but drivers behind a bus should not rely on those lights because they could be broken. [A04]
Why it matters: group school buses; misconception the lights always work.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0079]

FACT_ID: sec07-R12 | anchor: A06
During a police stop, turn the music down, avoid sudden movements, and do not reach for documents, the glove box, the console or under a seat unless told to, saying first what you are about to do. [A06]
Why it matters: group police stops; difficulty low.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0083]

FACT_ID: sec07-R13 | anchor: A07
If you disagree with a stop, do not argue at the roadside; you can contest the ticket later in court or file a complaint with the law enforcement agency. [A07]
Why it matters: group police stops; difficulty low.
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0084]

FACT_ID: sec07-R14 | anchor: A07
Follow the officer's instructions, including stepping out of the vehicle if asked, and politely ask for an instruction to be repeated if it is unclear. [A07]
Why it matters: group police stops; difficulty low.
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0084]

FACT_ID: sec07-R15 | anchor: A08
At night the pupils are dilated, and bright beams can blind other drivers for a moment by making their pupils constrict. [A08]
Why it matters: group headlights; difficulty medium.
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0085]

FACT_ID: sec07-R16 | anchor: A09
Taillights come on with the headlights and parking lights and grow brighter when the brakes are applied; in daylight they also light up when braking. [A09]
Why it matters: group vehicle lights; difficulty low.
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0086]

FACT_ID: sec07-R17 | anchor: A09
Interior overhead lights should be used only briefly while driving, or when a police officer asks you to light up the inside of a stopped vehicle. [A09]
Why it matters: group vehicle lights; difficulty low.
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0086]

FACT_ID: sec07-R18 | anchor: A09
Keep dashboard lights dim enough to avoid glare but bright enough to read the dials. [A09]
Why it matters: group vehicle lights; difficulty low.
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0086]

FACT_ID: sec07-R19 | anchor: A09
Spotlights and hazard flashers are for emergencies only, and spotlights may never be used for driving. [A09]
Why it matters: group vehicle lights; difficulty medium.
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0086]

FACT_ID: sec07-R20 | anchor: A09
Fog lights are auxiliary lights that may be used together with low beams to light the road ahead in foggy weather. [A09]
Why it matters: group vehicle lights; difficulty low.
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0086]

FACT_ID: sec07-R21 | anchor: A09
Before opening the driver-side door, check for traffic and for hard-to-see bicycles and mopeds, because a driver who opens a door into traffic may be liable for the crash; passengers should get out on the curb side. [A09]
Why it matters: group parking; difficulty medium.
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0086]

FACT_ID: sec07-R22 | anchor: A10
Never stop or park in a crosswalk, on a sidewalk, in a bus stop zone, in front of a driveway, inside an intersection, on an interstate, on a bridge, elevated roadway or in a tunnel, next to a car already parked at the curb, or in a disability space without authorization. [A10]
Why it matters: group parking; difficulty medium.
Source: [A10 -> pdf-0087]

FACT_ID: sec07-R23 | anchor: A10
If your vehicle has mechanical trouble or another emergency, stop on the right shoulder and turn on the emergency flashers. [A10]
Why it matters: group parking; difficulty low.
Source: [A10 -> pdf-0087]

FACT_ID: sec07-R24 | anchor: A11
To prove a handheld phone was used legally in an emergency, a driver may have to provide testimony or written statements from the authorities, or phone records. [A11]
Why it matters: group phones; difficulty high.
Source: [A11 -> pdf-0088]

FACT_ID: sec07-R25 | anchor: A11
Kulesh's, Kuberts' and Bolis' Law, enacted in 2012, treats illegal cell phone use while driving as recklessness under the vehicular homicide and assault by auto statutes. [A11]
Why it matters: group phones; difficulty high.
Source: [A11 -> pdf-0088]

FACT_ID: sec07-R26 | anchor: A11
A school bus driver may not use a handheld or hands-free phone while driving the bus, except in an emergency or when parked in a safe place off the highway. [A11]
Why it matters: group phones; confusable GDL versus school bus driver rule.
Source: [A11 -> pdf-0088]

FACT_ID: sec07-R27 | anchor: A12
Any trash, debris or rubbish carried in a vehicle must be covered so it cannot litter the road. [A12]
Why it matters: group littering; difficulty low.
Source: [A12 -> pdf-0089]
